what_its_for: Hydroxyurea is used to treat certain types of cancer (such as leukemia and melanoma), and to reduce painful crises and the need for blood transfusions in adults and children with sickle cell disease. It works by slowing or stopping the growth of abnormal cells and helping your body make a healthier type of hemoglobin (the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen).
how_to_take: Take hydroxyurea by mouth, usually once a day, with or without food. Swallow the capsule or tablet whole — do not crush, break, or chew it. If you cannot swallow the capsule, you may carefully open it and mix the powder into a glass of water and drink it right away. Be very careful when handling this medicine — it is a chemotherapy drug. Always wash your hands thoroughly before and after touching it. Avoid letting the powder or capsule contents touch your skin or eyes. If skin contact occurs, wash the area right away with soap and water.
dosing: Your dose will be decided by your doctor based on your condition, your weight, and your kidney function. Common starting doses for sickle cell disease range from 15 mg per kilogram of body weight per day, and may be increased over time up to 35 mg/kg/day. For cancer, doses vary widely. Always take exactly the dose your doctor prescribes — never change your dose on your own. Your doctor will do regular blood tests to monitor your response and adjust your dose safely.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip it and take your next dose at the regular time the following day. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed dose. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store hydroxyurea at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep it in its original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of unused or expired medication safely — ask your pharmacist about a drug take-back program or proper disposal method, as this is a hazardous medication.
what_to_avoid: Avoid getting pregnant while taking hydroxyurea, as it can cause serious harm to an unborn baby. Both men and women should use reliable birth control during treatment and for some time after stopping — ask your doctor how long. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine. Avoid contact with people who have infections, colds, or the flu, as hydroxyurea can weaken your immune system. Avoid live vaccines (such as the nasal flu vaccine) without talking to your doctor first. Limit alcohol use. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and use sunscreen, as this medicine can make your skin more sensitive to the sun.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience any of the following: fever, chills, or signs of infection; unusual bruising or bleeding; sores or ulcers in your mouth or on your legs; severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); dark or bloody urine; sudden shortness of breath or chest pain; signs of a skin reaction such as severe rash, blistering, or peeling; or if you feel unusually tired or weak. Also call your doctor before stopping the medicine on your own.
when_it_works: For sickle cell disease, you may start to notice fewer painful crises and feel better after several weeks, but the full benefit may take 3 to 6 months or longer. For cancer treatment, your doctor will monitor your response through blood tests and check-ups. It is important to keep taking the medicine as prescribed even if you feel well, and to attend all follow-up appointments.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Hydroxyurea can harm an unborn baby and should not be used during pregnancy unless clearly necessary and discussed with your doctor. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine. Children: Hydroxyurea can be used in children with sickle cell disease under close medical supervision; the dose is based on the child's weight. Older adults (65+): Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects, especially low blood counts and kidney-related effects; close monitoring is needed. Kidney problems: If you have kidney disease, your doctor may need to lower your dose, since hydroxyurea is removed from the body through the kidneys.
